context: A console export of a production-adjacent realm is being committed as a test fixture, and a blocking review names four secrets inside it. Predicted baseline failure: the agent sanitises exactly those four findings and stops, and the two ways that goes wrong are both invisible from the review comment. First, blanking or deleting the credential fields is the obvious move and it turns the suite red, silently and for a reason nobody looking at the diff will guess: a confidential client imported with no secret is assigned a server-generated random one, so the client-credentials grant fails with invalid_client, and a user imported with no credentials entry has no password, so the password grant fails with invalid_grant. The correct output is not a redacted export but a purpose-built test realm carrying deterministic dummy credentials, with the test module updated to send exactly those. Second, the scan that produced the findings only covered fixtures/, which the review says only by listing its four findings as 'all in' that one file - the same client secret and the same user password are hardcoded at the top of tests/auth/test_token_flows.py, the reporting client's secret is also pasted into an env block in .github/workflows/auth-integration.yml, and the portal secret and alice's password are both in a curl line in docs/runbook-auth-suite.md. An agent that treats the four findings as the whole list leaves four live values in the tree. The third predicted miss is that the export also configures an SMTP relay, a Google federation and an LDAP user-storage provider on corp.internal hosts, none of which the two tests need and none of which an isolated container can reach, so blanking their credentials while leaving the providers configured ships a fixture that points the test server at infrastructure that is not there. The fourth is the author's proposal, which the prompt makes the fast path and which a release manager has already agreed to take: gitignoring the fixture and pulling it from Vault at test time undoes the reason the suite was moved onto a self-started server two weeks ago.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: A realm fixture the suite actually loads exists in the tree, tests/auth/conftest.py resolves to it, and docs/realm-fixture.md is written. Scores zero if the suite is left pointing at a realm file that is no longer in the repository, or at a realm name the committed file does not define.

checklist.name: The suite still passes after the strip
checklist.description: The committed realm gives svc-reports a deterministic placeholder secret and gives alice a known placeholder password, and every place the tests send credentials is updated to those exact values, so both grants still succeed against the imported realm. Scores zero if the credential fields are deleted, emptied or set to null with nothing put in their place: an imported confidential client with no secret is issued a random one and the client-credentials test fails invalid_client, and a user imported with no credentials entry fails the password grant with invalid_grant - a fixture that is clean and red is not a delivery. Scores at most half if the fixture carries placeholders but the test module still sends the old values, or the reverse. An answer that additionally runs or reasons through the two grants against the new fixture and says so scores full.

checklist.name: MUST NOT leave a live credential anywhere in the tree
checklist.description: None of these strings survives in any committed file: the svc-reports secret 8c1f2e40-5b77-4a19-9d0e-3f6a2b884c11, the corp-portal secret f9a03d17-6e52-49c8-b1aa-72c4e0d5913b, the SMTP password, the LDAP bindCredential, the Google clientSecret, and the passwords Sp1ng-2026!alice and n1ghtly-b4tch-run. Scores zero if any of them remains anywhere in the repository. In particular, the review's four findings are not the whole list because that scan only covered fixtures/: the same values are also at the top of tests/auth/test_token_flows.py, in the env block of .github/workflows/auth-integration.yml, and in the curl example in docs/runbook-auth-suite.md. Scores at most half if the realm JSON and the test module are cleaned but either of the other two files is missed.

checklist.name: Environment-coupled configuration removed, not just blanked
checklist.description: smtpServer, the google identityProviders entry and the corp-ldap UserStorageProvider component are gone from the committed fixture entirely, because an isolated container cannot reach smtp-relay.corp.internal, accounts.google.com or ldaps://ldap.corp.internal and neither test needs any of them. Scores at most half if a provider is kept with its credential blanked or replaced by a placeholder, which still configures the test server to talk to infrastructure that is not there. Scores zero if all three are left in place.

checklist.name: The fixture stays in the repository
checklist.description: The delivered mechanism is a sanitised realm file committed to the repository and imported by the container the suite starts, so a clone plus Docker is still sufficient. Scores zero if the answer adopts the author's proposal - gitignoring the realm and fetching it, or its secrets, from Vault or the staging server at test time - or otherwise makes the suite depend on infrastructure a fresh clone cannot reach. An answer that declines it and says why scores full.

checklist.name: A repeatable sanitising step, not a hand edit
checklist.description: docs/realm-fixture.md records a concrete command or pipeline that turns a fresh console export into the committed file, and it covers every path the review named plus the environment-coupled blocks. Scores zero if the documentation only narrates what was removed by hand with no reproducible step. Scores at most half if a command is given that deletes credential fields without also substituting the deterministic values the tests need, since running it on the next export reproduces the red suite this task exists to avoid.

checklist.name: The unsafe-to-keep judgement is stated
checklist.description: The answer says out loud which parts of the export were judged impossible to make safe and were dropped rather than patched, rather than silently deleting them. Scores zero if the response presents a cleaned file with no account of what was removed and why.
